title: 2 Kings 19:14–19
context: Hezekiah takes the Assyrian letter, goes up to the LORD’s house, and spreads it before the LORD. His prayer confesses the LORD as the God of Israel enthroned above the cherubim, the only God of all the kingdoms of the earth and the maker of heaven and earth, and asks him to hear Sennacherib’s defiance. Hezekiah admits that Assyria has destroyed the nations and their gods, which were no gods but the work of men’s hands, and he asks the LORD to save Judah so that all kingdoms may know that he alone is God. The same prayer appears in Isaiah 37:14–20. Arminian and Reformed readers commonly read this prayer as shared ground: a model of bringing threats to God, grounding requests in his character, and seeking his glory among the nations.

verses.text: Hezekiah received the letter from the hand of the messengers and read it. Then Hezekiah went up to the LORD’s house, and spread it before the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Hezekiah reading the letter, going up to the LORD’s house, and spreading it before the LORD. He brings the threat directly to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the spread-out letter as a vivid picture of casting cares on God (compare 1 Peter 5:7). Readers in both traditions commonly treat the verse as a model for prayer in crisis.

verses.text: Hezekiah prayed before the LORD, and said, “LORD, the God of Israel, enthroned above the cherubim, you are the God, even you alone, of all the kingdoms of the earth. You have made heaven and earth.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Hezekiah addressing the LORD as enthroned above the cherubim, the only God of all kingdoms, and the maker of heaven and earth. Prayer begins with who God is.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the confession of God’s sole sovereignty as the ground of the request (compare Psalm 80:1). Both traditions commonly hold up the verse as a pattern for beginning prayer with worship.

verses.text: Incline your ear, LORD, and hear. Open your eyes, LORD, and see. Hear the words of Sennacherib, which he has sent to defy the living God.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Hezekiah asking the LORD to incline his ear, open his eyes, and hear Sennacherib’s defiance. He appeals to God’s attentive care.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the plea as rooted in God’s concern for his own name against those who defy the living God. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as bold, reverent petition.

verses.text: Truly, LORD, the kings of Assyria have laid waste the nations and their lands,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Hezekiah honestly admitting that the kings of Assyria have laid waste the nations. Faith does not deny hard facts.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the admission as truthful realism within prayer. Both traditions commonly read the verse as showing that trust in God can coexist with a clear view of danger.

verses.text: and have cast their gods into the fire; for they were no gods, but the work of men’s hands, wood and stone. Therefore they have destroyed them.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Hezekiah explaining that the conquered gods were no gods but the work of human hands. Their destruction proves nothing about the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as a sharp contrast between idols and the living God (compare Psalm 115:4). Readers in both traditions commonly read it as the answer to the Assyrian boast.

verses.text: Now therefore, LORD our God, save us, I beg you, out of his hand, that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that you, LORD, are God alone.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Hezekiah asking the LORD to save Judah so that all kingdoms may know he alone is God. His request reaches beyond Judah’s survival to God’s glory.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the request as aligning the prayer with God’s own purpose to be known among the nations. Both traditions commonly hold up the verse as a model of praying for God’s name above all.
